Section 01How to read a review as a connected theory

A collective optical spectrum is measured from many molecules at once, whereas a chemical reaction usually happens at a particular molecule. The central difficulty is to connect those two descriptions without confusing a collective enhancement with a large local perturbation. This review organizes several answers: coherent light–matter hybridization, reduced diagonal environmental fluctuations, relaxation through a large dark manifold, competition between electron transfer and photon loss, and a vibrational energy-flow mechanism for ground-state reactions.

These are related ideas, but they are not one universal mechanism. The same factor of 1/N can describe a local transition probability, a variance, or a particular final-state matrix element. Summing over final states, changing which quantity is held fixed, or measuring a conditional observable can completely change the apparent scaling.

The aim of these notes is to work through the connecting mathematics. Exact finite-dimensional identities are separated from weak-bath rate theory, classical Marcus theory, an empirical linewidth interpolation, and a proposed kinetic explanation of vibrational strong coupling. A result established for one of these models is not automatically a statement about every polaritonic material.

Primary source: W. Ying, M. E. Mondal, E. R. Koessler, S. Montillo Vega, and P. Huo, Collective Effects in Polariton Chemistry and Photophysics, Annual Review of Physical Chemistry 77, 201–224 (2026). Read the review. Equations in this tutorial have their own numbering. Small matrix examples, conservation checks, and the susceptibility derivation below are tutorial developments, not new experimental claims.

Section 02Source map, units, and notation

The review uses a compact notation in which frequencies and their corresponding energies often appear together. Here, Ex, Ec, gn, G, λ, and W denote energies unless a section explicitly switches to mass-weighted oscillator frequencies. Thus a collective on-resonance splitting is 2G, and a photon population decay rate is κ=W/ℏ. The molecular fraction of a polariton is always denoted w; this avoids ambiguities caused by exchanging sine and cosine mixing-angle conventions.

Review location Main question Tutorial route
Section 2, journal pp. 204–208 What is the model and what becomes collective? Tensor products, bright/dark matrices, loss, bath projection
Section 3, pp. 208–211 Why do relaxation, coherence, and linewidths scale differently? Channel counting, thermal factors, kinetic generator, spectra
Section 4, pp. 211–213 How can local electron transfer retain a collective dependence? Local acceptors, summed rates, Marcus activation, competing losses
Section 5, pp. 214–218 How can a cavity change an energy-flow bottleneck? Pauli–Fierz coordinate square, bright oscillator, susceptibility, rate overlap
Section 6, p. 218 Which problems remain open? Validity conditions and connections to the other Deep Dives

An operator acting on a quantum Hilbert space carries a hat. When a list of classical coordinates or populations is written as a ket, it is a vector in an ordinary coordinate or probability space, not a quantum superposition. We state the relevant basis when moving between these spaces.

Section 03The microscopic Hilbert space and local operators

Let molecule n have electronic ground and excited states |gn⟩ and |en⟩, and let the cavity have Fock states |q⟩c. Each molecule also has its own nuclear or phonon Hilbert space. Before truncation the space is

H=(⨂n=1Nspan{|gn⟩,|en⟩})⊗Fc⊗(⨂n=1NHb,n).
(1)

In the ordered local electronic basis (|gn⟩,|en⟩), define

[σ^n−]g,e=(0100),[σ^n+]g,e=(0010),[n^n]g,e=(0001),n^n=σ^n+σ^n−.
(2)

The full operator σ^n− means this matrix tensored with identities on all other molecules, the cavity, and the baths. The photon operator instead has a^|q⟩c=q|q−1⟩c. Its ladder is not a hard-core molecular ladder. This distinction becomes essential beyond one excitation.

The vacuum |G⟩ has all molecules in their electronic ground states and no photon. We use |c⟩=a^†|G⟩ and |En⟩=σ^n+|G⟩ for the one-excitation states. Nuclear identities are suppressed only after the system and bath operators have been separated.

Section 04Tavis–Cummings coupling and its approximations

Within the rotating-wave, single-mode model, choose the coupling convention

H^S=Eca^†a^+∑nExn^n+∑n(gnσ^n+a^+gn∗a^†σ^n−).
(3)

It conserves N^ex=a^†a^+∑nn^n. In the ordered basis B1=(|c⟩,|E1⟩,…,|EN⟩), its matrix is

[H^S]B1=(Ecg1∗g2∗⋯gN∗g1Ex0⋯0g20Ex⋯0⋮⋮⋮⋱⋮gN00⋯Ex).
(4)

This is an effective excitation Hamiltonian. It does not include counter-rotating terms or a separately retained dipole self-energy. Its use must be justified in the excitation regime being modeled; it is not a general ground-state Pauli–Fierz Hamiltonian. Later, for vibrational reaction kinetics, the review deliberately changes to a coordinate Hamiltonian containing the dipole self-energy. Importing conclusions across that change without inspecting the Hamiltonian would be unsafe.

Section 05Bright-state construction without guessing a mixing angle

Define the collective energy G=(∑n|gn|2)1/2. For G>0, the normalized bright ket is

|B⟩=1G∑ngn|En⟩,P^B=|B⟩⟨B|,P^D=∑n|En⟩⟨En|−P^B.
(5)

Acting with the Hamiltonian verifies H^S|c⟩=Ec|c⟩+G|B⟩ and H^S|B⟩=G|c⟩+Ex|B⟩. Every normalized molecular ket orthogonal to |B⟩ is uncoupled from the photon in this ideal identical-energy model. The projector P^D has rank N−1.

Choose orthonormal dark states |D1⟩,…,|DN−1⟩. In (|c⟩,|B⟩,|D1⟩,…),

[H^S]c,B,D=(EcGGEx)⊕ExI^N−1.
(6)

The reduction to one bright state is exact for this rank-one coupling and degenerate molecular block. Disorder in molecular energies generally couples the bright state to the dark subspace. Calling an instantaneous disordered eigenstate “dark” then means mostly molecular or weakly optically active, not exactly zero photon amplitude.

Section 06A complete two-molecule change of basis

For identical real g1=g2=g, use |B⟩=(|E1⟩+|E2⟩)/2 and |D⟩=(|E1⟩−|E2⟩)/2. The columns of the transformation matrix are the new basis kets expressed in the old basis:

[U^](c,E1,E2)←(c,B,D)=(10001/21/201/2−1/2),U^†[H^S]B1U^=(Ec2g02gEx000Ex).
(7)

At resonance Ec=Ex, define |+⟩=(|c⟩+|B⟩)/2 and |−⟩=(|c⟩−|B⟩)/2. Their molecular amplitudes are (1/2,1/2) and (−1/2,−1/2), respectively. The dark amplitudes are (1/2,−1/2). This explicit example will let us test bath-induced transitions instead of relying on verbal descriptions of decoupling.

Section 07Polariton energies and composition

The characteristic polynomial of the bright block is (E−Ec)(E−Ex)−G2=0. Writing δ=Ec−Ex and D=δ2+4G2,

E±=Ec+Ex±D2,w+=12(1−δD),w−=12(1+δD).
(8)

Here w±=∑n|⟨En|±⟩|2 are molecular probabilities; the photon probabilities are 1−w±. One check is the positive-detuning limit: if the photon energy lies far above the exciton energy, the upper state becomes photonic, so w+→0. This check is more reliable than memorizing whether a particular author assigns sine or cosine to the upper polariton.

For uniform couplings, |⟨En|±⟩|2=w±/N. The local excitation probability is small even when the full eigenstate has order-one molecular character.

Section 08What changes when there is more than one cavity mode?

For multiple modes, the molecule–photon coupling is a matrix V^ with entries Vnα=gnαeikαxn. Its singular value decomposition identifies independent bright molecular combinations. If r=rankV^, the coupling-null molecular subspace has dimension N−r, before energetic disorder mixes it with the optically active subspace.

A single-mode N−1 dark-state count is therefore not transferable without modification to spatial transport in a multimode cavity. On a periodic uniform lattice, the natural molecular bright combinations are Fourier kets, one for each retained photonic wavevector. The corresponding 2×2 blocks have wavevector-dependent photon energies. The 2025 transport Deep Dive derives those FFT transformations, and the 2026 atomistic tutorial explains how time-dependent molecular transition dipoles enter them.

Section 09Loss: a rate, a width, and a complex pole are different objects

Let κ denote the photon population decay rate, in inverse time. The trace-preserving cavity dissipator is

dρ^dt=−iℏ[H^S,ρ^]+κ(a^ρ^a^†−12{a^†a^,ρ^}).
(9)

An isolated cavity population decays as e−κt, its optical coherence as e−κt/2, and its Lorentzian energy FWHM is W=ℏκ. These factors of two cannot be interchanged.

For an undriven one-excitation ket, loss can be propagated with H^eff=H^S−iW|c⟩⟨c|/2, provided lost probability is assigned to |G⟩. The non-Hermitian excited block is not by itself a normalized density operator. It is an exact representation of this particular single-excitation loss problem along a prescribed system Hamiltonian, not a general replacement for the recycling term in nonlinear spectroscopy.

Section 10Pole splitting is not the same as two resolvable peaks

Assign a phenomenological bare molecular FWHM Γ and photon FWHM W. The complex bright-block eigenvalues are

E±=Ec+Ex2−i(W+Γ)4±G2+14[δ−i(W−Γ)2]2.
(10)

At resonance, the square root becomes G2−(W−Γ)2/16. Thus unequal loss rates yield a real-pole splitting only beyond G>|W−Γ|/4. But a nonzero real splitting can still be smaller than the peak widths; in that case two peaks need not be resolved. Peak visibility additionally depends on excitation/detection channels and interference.

The review discusses strong coupling and delocalization criteria for particular disordered models. They are useful diagnostics, not a proof that any spectrum with two humps contains a delocalized molecular state of known participation size. Spectral splitting, state delocalization, coherence time, and chemical yield are separate tests.

Section 11Local baths in the polariton basis

Use an independent bath force B^n on each molecular excitation:

H^SB=∑nn^n⊗B^n,⟨B^n(t)B^m(0)⟩=δnmC(t).
(11)

For eigenstates |α⟩, define unα=⟨En|α⟩. Then ⟨α|H^SB|β⟩=∑nunα∗unβB^n. The same molecular projector generates both diagonal noise and off-diagonal transitions.

In the resonant two-molecule basis (|+⟩,|−⟩,|D⟩), the local system coupling matrices are

[n^1]+,−,D=(1/4−1/41/(22)−1/41/4−1/(22)1/(22)−1/(22)1/2),[n^2]+,−,D=(1/4−1/4−1/(22)−1/41/41/(22)−1/(22)1/(22)1/2).
(12)

The upper–dark element is (B^1−B^2)/(22), while each polariton diagonal element is (B^1+B^2)/4. Independent baths therefore leave a difference-noise transition channel even when the diagonal average becomes small. Replacing two independent baths by one common bath changes the model.

Section 12Deriving the collective reorganization energy

Let qn=|unα|2 be a polariton’s molecular probability at site n. A local harmonic bath potential with linear coupling cjQ^nj is displaced by −qncj/(mjωj2) on that projected branch. Completing its square gives

λα=∑n,jqn2cj22mjωj2=λ∑nqn2,λ±=λw±2N,λ±|δ=0=λ4N.
(13)

There are two reductions at resonance: the total molecular probability is one half, and that probability is distributed over N independent environments. Squaring the local weights before summing is essential. Summing the weights first would predict λ/4, missing the spatial averaging.

This is a projected diagonal coupling result. It does not set the off-diagonal entries of the preceding bath matrices to zero and does not say that all nuclear effects disappear from polariton dynamics.

Section 13Correlated environments and participation size

The variance of a weighted fluctuation δEα=∑nqnδϵn is the quadratic form ⟨q|Σ^|q⟩, with Σnm=⟨δϵnδϵm⟩. Here |q⟩ is a real vector of probability weights in site-index space.

For equal local variances σ2 and a common correlation coefficient r, uniform weights qn=w/N give

Var(δEα)=σ2w2[r+1−rN].
(14)

The independent-bath result is recovered at r=0; a fully common fluctuation at r=1 is not averaged away. This covariance matrix is physical only for −1/(N−1)≤r≤1.

For nonuniform weights, define Npart=w2/∑nqn2 when w>0. Then independent identical baths give λα=λw2/Npart. A large number of molecules in the simulation box is not enough: the particular state must actually spread its molecular weight across them.

Section 14Deriving the thermal factors in transition rates

Take a harmonic bath B^n=∑jbj(b^nj+b^nj†). In energy units define J(E)=π∑jbj2δ(E−ℏωj). For E>0, its quantum correlation contains (n¯E+1)e−iEt/ℏ from emission and n¯Ee+iEt/ℏ from absorption, with n¯E=(eE/kBT−1)−1.

The second-order long-time transition rate is the Fourier transform of that correlation at the system energy difference. Defining Ξβα=∑n|unβ|2|unα|2, one obtains

kα→β↓=2ℏΞβαJ(ΔE)[n¯ΔE+1],kβ→α↑=2ℏΞβαJ(ΔE)n¯ΔE,ΔE=Eα−Eβ>0.
(15)

The factor 2/ℏ follows from the stated π-normalized spectral density and the full time Fourier integral. Other conventions move factors into J. The unambiguous check is k↑/k↓=e−ΔE/kBT.

These formulas assume weak residual coupling, a stationary thermal environment, and an appropriate long-time/secular rate description. The review also points to nonequilibrium time-dependent rates. An initially displaced bath or a strongly non-Markovian transient is not automatically described by the equilibrium constants above.

Section 15Why a large dark manifold defeats naive one-over-N reasoning

For equal couplings, a normalized dark ket has ∑n|unD|2=1. Consequently the overlap for one polariton–dark pair is ΞD,+=w+/N. Summing the N−1 orthogonal final dark states gives

k+→D=2ℏN−1Nw+J(Δ+)[n¯Δ++1],k−→D=2ℏN−1Nw−J(Δ−)n¯Δ−,kD→−=2ℏw−NJ(Δ−)[n¯Δ−+1],Δ+=E+−Ex,Δ−=Ex−E−.
(16)

Here PD will denote the total population of a normalized dark-manifold state or mixture, not the population in each dark state separately. There is no N−1 multiplier on kD→−: the final state is one lower polariton. An isotropic dark mixture is represented by ρ^D=P^D/(N−1), not by the unnormalized P^D.

Thermal-factor check. The printed review’s Equation 13c uses n¯ for the downward dark-to-lower-polariton process. The downward process requires n¯+1 with the positive gap used there. The equations and teaching code here use the emission factor and satisfy detailed balance. This is a convention check against the bath correlation, not a new relaxation mechanism. Compare the printed equation.

At fixed G, k+→D approaches a finite value as N→∞, while the diagonal reorganization energy approaches zero. These statements coexist without contradiction because they involve different matrix-element sums.

Section 16A probability-conserving kinetic matrix

Use the ordered population-space basis (|U⟩pop,|D⟩pop,|L⟩pop,|G⟩pop), and write the column |p⟩pop=(PU,PD,PL,PG)T. For clarity, only the population column is a probability vector, not a state ket. Let kUD,kDU,kLD,kDL describe upper/dark and lower/dark transitions, and let κU=κ(1−w+), κL=κ(1−w−). Then

ddt|p⟩pop=K^|p⟩pop,[K^]U,D,L,G=(−kUD−κUkDU00kUD−kDU−kDLkLD00kDL−kLD−κL0κU0κL0).
(17)

Every column sums to zero. All off-diagonal entries are nonnegative. Therefore ⟨1|K^=0 preserves the total probability. Optional molecular nonradiative channels can be added as paired loss/gain entries. An absorbing ground state makes the ultimate stationary state trivial; apparent upper/dark/lower equilibrium is a conditional or pre-loss notion, not the final state of this lossy model.

The branch-specific leakage rates use a secular polariton approximation. Exact bare-cavity Lindblad propagation also carries coherences between polaritons and is preferable when their splitting is not large compared with the dissipative rates.

Section 17Dark-state entropy as a degeneracy count

Switch off the irreversible losses and suppose dark levels are degenerate at Ex. Detailed balance with the total dark population gives

PDeqPLeq=(N−1)e−Δ−/kBT,ΔFD−L=Δ−−kBTln⁡(N−1).
(18)

The factor is a degeneracy of one-excitation final states, not a count of N−1 simultaneously excited particles. For N=101, T=300 K, and Δ−=50 meV, the ratio is approximately 14.5, even though each dark level lies above the lower polariton. A single state can be thermally disfavored while the entire manifold is favored.

Energetic disorder replaces (N−1)e−βEx by ∑je−βEDj. Nonequilibrium pumping and irreversible decay generally prevent assigning this equilibrium ratio to a measured transient without a kinetic calculation.

Section 18Polariton coherence and its remaining decay channels

For resolved polaritons in a weak-coupling secular description, population escape from either state removes their mutual coherence. A useful accounting equation is

dρ+−dt≃[−iDℏ−k+→D+k−→D2−κ2−γφ+−]ρ+−.
(19)

The cavity term is κ[(1−w+)+(1−w−)]/2=κ/2, because the two ideal branches exhaust the bright two-state block. Additional molecular population losses and direct interbranch transitions contribute further half-sums of escape rates. This expression is an approximation to the full dissipative dynamics, not a substitute for it at near-degenerate or strongly broadened parameters.

Diagonal gap fluctuations involve ∑n(|un+|2−|un−|2)B^n. At exact resonance these weights cancel in the ideal uniform model: both branch energies experience the same first-order diagonal noise. That does not eliminate bath-induced off-diagonal transitions. It also does not eliminate ground-to-polariton optical dephasing, which compares one polariton to a different, unexcited state.

The PNAS Deep Dive explains how waiting-time cross-peak oscillations reveal mutual coherence and why that signal must be distinguished from population relaxation and optical linewidth.

Section 19Absorption, time-domain decay, and a linewidth interpolation

For a dipole μ^ and equilibrium density operator ρ^eq, a common absorption convention is proportional to Re∫0∞eiωtCμ(t)dt, with Cμ(t)=Tr[μ^(t)μ^ρ^eq]. If one isolated component is C0e−iω0t−γt, then

Re∫0∞ei(ω−ω0)t−γtdt=γγ2+(ω−ω0)2,FWHME=2ℏγ.
(20)

The review contrasts simple Hopfield-weighted molecular broadening with the nonlinear linewidths found in numerical simulations. In the unambiguous molecular-fraction notation used here, its Equation 16 is

Γ−fit=(1−w−)W+w−2/N1−w−+w−2/NΓ,Γ+fit=(1−w+)W+w+2/N1−w++w+2/NΓ+ℏk+→D.
(21)

This is a reported interpolation fitted to finite-ensemble HEOM results, not a general identity derivable merely by replacing λ with λ/(4N). At resonance its matter prefactor is 1/(2N+1). Slow Gaussian fluctuations instead produce a width proportional to the square root of their variance, whereas fast Lorentzian broadening is proportional to the variance times a memory time. The 2024 motional-narrowing notes derive those limits.

Adding a fitted relaxation term and a separately computed dissipative width requires checking for double counting. One should not add the same escape mechanism twice because it appeared under two different names.

Section 20A scaling map: specify both the observable and the limit

Quantity, for an ideal uniformly delocalized one-excitation state At fixed collective energy G Qualification
Individual light–matter matrix element g=G/N Not the same limit as fixed mode volume and fixed g
Molecular probability on one site w/N State-specific; localization changes it
Projected independent-bath reorganization λw2/N Common fluctuations do not average away
Upper-to-one-dark overlap w+/N One specified normalized final ket
Upper-to-all-dark overlap w+(N−1)/N Remains finite at large N
Polariton-to-one-local-acceptor coupling squared w+|VDA|2/N One electronic transfer channel
Sum over all local acceptors w+|VDA|2 No dilution prefactor, but activation and loss still matter

At fixed individual coupling instead, G∝N, so energy gaps, Bose occupations, and spectral-density values all change. A measured N-dependence cannot be interpreted until this distinction is specified.

Section 21A donor–acceptor model in an explicit basis

To discuss photochemistry, let each molecule have a photoexcited donor configuration |dn⟩ and an acceptor configuration |an⟩. Lowercase d here labels a chemical donor, not an optical dark state. Local electron transfer has ⟨an|H^|dm⟩=VDAδnm, while only the donor excitation couples strongly to the cavity.

For two molecules, in the ordered basis (|c⟩,|d1⟩,|d2⟩,|a1⟩,|a2⟩), a real-coupling example is

[H^]c,d1,d2,a1,a2=(Ecgg00gED0VDA0g0ED0VDA0VDA0EA000VDA0EA).
(22)

Separate harmonic solvent coordinates shift the donor and acceptor free-energy surfaces. The electronic energies and the solvent displacements must be defined consistently to avoid counting the reorganization shift both in the vertical energy and in the surface minimum.

Section 22Why summing local electron-transfer channels removes dilution

Suppose the prepared upper polariton has molecular amplitudes w+/N, up to phases. The matrix element into one local acceptor is VDAw+/N. Because distinct local acceptor final states are orthogonal, their probabilities add in the rate expression:

∑n=1N|⟨an|H^|+⟩|2=∑n=1Nw+|VDA|2N=w+|VDA|2.
(23)

There is no overall 1/N penalty in that total transition rate. This does not predict order-one chemical conversion at every molecule after a single excitation: the total probability is shared among the acceptors. Nor does the cancellation alone guarantee acceleration. The activation energy, phonon overlap, initial preparation, and competing decay rates determine the observed conversion.

This channel sum is an instructive counterpart to upper-to-dark scattering. In both cases, a small matrix element to each final ket need not imply a small total rate into an extensive manifold.

Section 23Deriving the Marcus rate and its polariton shift

In the classical harmonic-solvent limit, the energy-gap distribution sampled on the initial surface is Gaussian. Let x be the final-minus-initial electronic energy gap. Its mean is ΔG+λA and its variance is 2λAkBT. The probability density at a crossing, x=0, is

P(0)=14πλAkBTexp⁡[−(ΔG+λA)24λAkBT].
(24)

Fermi’s golden rule multiplies this density by 2π|V|2/ℏ. Preparing the upper polariton raises the initial electronic energy relative to the donor by ΔE+=(δ+D)/2, and the summed coupling factor is w+|VDA|2. Therefore the review’s large-ensemble rate becomes

k+→A=2πℏw+|VDA|24πλAkBTexp⁡[−(ΔG−ΔE++λA)24λAkBT].
(25)

The apparent collective dependence enters through ΔE+ and w+, rather than a bare N multiplier. The activationless condition is ΔG−ΔE++λA=0. Pushing further can enter the Marcus inverted regime. Consequently “larger splitting gives faster chemistry” is not a general statement.

The derivation assumes weak donor–acceptor coupling, a suitable thermal solvent distribution, and a classical Gaussian description. Quantized high-frequency accepting modes, initially nonequilibrated solvent motion, or strong nonadiabatic mixing require a more detailed theory. Compare review Equation 18.

Section 24A finite-size reorganization check

It is useful to see why donor reorganization can disappear from the large-ensemble activation energy but remain important for relaxation. Suppose identical independent solvent modes have donor displacement RD and local acceptor displacement RA. On a projected uniform initial polariton surface, every coordinate is shifted by w+RD/N. On final local acceptor an, only coordinate n is shifted by RA. The squared displacement difference sums to

λeff=λA−2w+Nsgn(RARD)λAλD+w+2NλD.
(26)

This is a tutorial harmonic-surface calculation: subtract the initial and final coordinate shifts, square each difference, and sum the N independent mode energies. It tends to λA as N→∞. It assumes a projected branch with coordinate-independent composition and identical curvatures; it is not a general finite-size formula for a strongly distorted adiabatic polariton surface.

Meanwhile, λD controls the donor bath spectral density that produces upper-to-dark transitions. A small donor contribution to one activation barrier does not mean that donor phonons can be omitted from the kinetic competition.

Section 25A reaction rate is not a photochemical yield

Treat electron transfer, dark transfer, and photon loss as three absorbing escape channels from a prepared upper state, with rates kA, kD, and kc=κ(1−w+). Then PU(t)=e−(kA+kD+kc)t, and integrating product flux gives

YA(∞)=∫0∞kAPU(t)dt=kAkA+kD+kc.
(27)

For example, kA=1, kD=4, and kc=5 in the same inverse-time units yield only 10% product, despite a finite electron-transfer rate. Doubling kA raises the yield to 2/11, not to 20%. Dark-state return, acceptor relaxation, and reversible chemistry require an expanded kinetic matrix rather than this three-escape formula.

The review considers resonant continuous-wave pumping to replenish upper-polariton population against loss. Pumping changes the population supply and steady flux; it does not remove loss from the microscopic generator. Comparing pumped and unpumped experiments requires matching absorbed flux, excitation density, and the reported observable.

Section 26Detuning: competing benefits and penalties

Positive cavity detuning makes the upper branch more photonic and moves it farther above the dark manifold. This can suppress phonon-assisted relaxation if the bath has little weight at the increased gap. But the same change reduces the molecular factor w+ in electron transfer and increases upper-branch photon loss. It also changes the Marcus driving force, which may help or hurt depending on the activation regime.

The review’s detuning-dependent results illustrate this competition. A useful computational analysis should plot at least the individual rates, the molecular/photon fractions, and the final yield—not just one effective fitted rate. At large detuning, the label “upper polariton” remains an eigenvalue label, but its chemical content can become very small.

Section 27Worked collective-scale example and calculator

Take N=101, G=50 meV, zero detuning, T=300 K, and λ=6.2 meV. Each polariton has half molecular character; its projected reorganization is 6.2/(4×101)≃0.01535 meV. Yet the total upper-to-dark overlap is (100/101)/2≃0.495, not 0.5/101. The dark/lower equilibrium ratio is approximately 14.5 for the resulting 50 meV gap. These numbers expose the difference between fluctuation averaging, transition-channel counting, and entropy.

The following calculator uses the stated energy convention, a Drude spectral density J(E)=2λγE/(γ2+E2), the equilibrium FGR expressions above, and the simplified Marcus/absorbing-branch model. The resulting yield is a teaching calculation, not a fit to a particular experiment.

Collective probabilities, rates, and reaction competition

Section 28Vibrational strong coupling requires a different Hamiltonian

The review’s ground-state reaction model consists of a reactive coordinate R^0, spectator vibrations R^n, and a photon displacement q^c. The spectators are rate-promoting modes coupled to the reaction coordinate; they are not additional electronic donor states. We now use mass-weighted coordinates and the review’s ℏ=1 oscillator convention. Every ω, damping coefficient, and parameter a in this oscillator subsection is an inverse-time frequency. A calculator may consistently express all of them in the same spectroscopic wavenumber scale because it reports only dimensionless ratios.

Including the coordinate-square terms, the model is

H^=H^0(R^0,P^0)+∑n[P^n22+ω022(R^n−Cnω02R^0)2]+p^c22+ωc22(q^c+2ωcηc∑nR^n)2+H^residual baths.
(28)

Here H^0=P^02/2+V(R^0) contains the reaction barrier. Expanding the last square generates both the bilinear photon–spectator coupling and the dipole self-energy. Expanding the spectator squares generates the reaction-coordinate counterterm. Omitting either while keeping the other terms gives a different model. Compare review Equation 19.

Section 29Which spectator combination couples to the reaction coordinate?

For identical spectator frequencies, define the cavity-bright coordinate R^B=N−1/2∑nR^n. Orthogonal combinations are dark with respect to this one cavity mode. The reactive interaction is −R^0∑nCnR^n. It couples purely to R^B only if the reaction-coupling vector is parallel to the optical-coupling vector.

For a more general optical vector |g⟩ and reaction vector |C⟩ in spectator-index space, define

χ=|⟨g|C⟩|2⟨g|g⟩⟨C|C⟩,0≤χ≤1.
(29)

The reaction-coupling norm splits into a bright part χ⟨C|C⟩ and a dark part (1−χ)⟨C|C⟩. The cavity can strongly split the optical bright mode while the reaction continues through the uncoupled dark component. This overlap is a sharper statement than simply saying there are many spectator molecules.

As a simple disorder check, a fixed uniform reaction vector and statistically isotropic, uncorrelated optical orientations generally have only an order-1/N squared projection. Correlations between solvent orientation, the reactive coupling, and local structure can change that conclusion. The aligned-spectator model should therefore not be advertised as a proof that arbitrary isotropic solutions have the same collective kinetic effect.

Section 30An explicit oscillator matrix with the dipole self-energy

Set a2=2Nηc2ωc. Holding the reaction coordinate aside, the bright/photon potential in the ordered coordinate basis (RB,qc) is 12⟨Q|K^|Q⟩, where |Q⟩=(RB,qc)T is an ordinary mass-weighted coordinate vector and

[K^]B,c=(ω02+a2aωcaωcωc2),detK^=ω02ωc2>0.
(30)

The added a2 is the bright-sector dipole self-energy. The squared normal-mode frequencies are

ω±2=12[ω02+ωc2+a2±(ω02+a2−ωc2)2+4a2ωc2].
(31)

At resonance ωc=ω0, their product obeys ω+ω−=ω02, and their exact difference is ω+−ω−=a. Their average shifts upward; the familiar ω0±a/2 form is the leading weak-coupling expansion, not the exact eigenvalue formula of this coordinate-square Hamiltonian.

The determinant check is especially useful. Without the self-energy, the determinant would become ω02ωc2−a2ωc2, and sufficiently large coupling would create an artificial instability in the truncated oscillator model.

Section 31Eliminate the photon by a Schur complement

Add Markovian damping γ to the spectator and κc to the cavity. These are the coefficients multiplying −iω in the inverse oscillator response, not the optical energy widths used earlier. With the Fourier convention e−iωt, the driven response satisfies

(ω02+a2−ω2−iγωaωcaωcωc2−ω2−iκcω)(RB(ω)qc(ω))=(F(ω)0).
(32)

The second row gives qc=−aωcRB/(ωc2−ω2−iκcω). Substituting it into the first row gives

XBB(ω)=RB(ω)F(ω)=1ω02+a2−ω2−iγω−a2ωc2ωc2−ω2−iκcω.
(33)

This algebra is exact for the stated two damped linear oscillators. It has not yet assumed a rotating-wave splitting or an activated chemical rate. The poles explain the hybrid vibrational response; a rate needs the overlap of that response with the reactive transition.

Section 32Separate the dispersive shift from the effective damping

Multiply the photon denominator by its complex conjugate. With Dc=(ωc2−ω2)2+κc2ω2, the response takes the form

XBB(ω)=1ω02−ω2+Π(ω)−iωΓR(ω),Π(ω)=a2ω2(ω2−ωc2+κc2)Dc,ΓR(ω)=γ+a2ωc2κcDc.
(34)

Its positive-frequency imaginary part is

ImXBB(ω)=ωΓR(ω)[ω02−ω2+Π(ω)]2+[ωΓR(ω)]2.
(35)

Using a2=2Nηc2ωc gives the frequency-dependent terms printed below the review’s Equation 22. Their phenomenological intrinsic spectator damping is written there as 2λR/γR. We keep it as the independently specified coefficient γ rather than mixing it with the electronic Drude parameters from earlier sections.

The review uses a reaction-weighted spectral factor Jrev(ω)=Λω02ImXBB(ω), where Λ=∑nCn2/(2ω02). An alternative definition based directly on force-response strength would use (∑nCn2)ImX, differing by two. The rate prefactor must match the chosen convention. Ratios computed with the same convention do not depend on this common normalization.

Section 33Rate suppression is a spectral-overlap calculation

Let |νL⟩→|νL′⟩ be the thermally activated reactant-well transition at frequency ω0, with coordinate matrix element Δ=⟨νL|R^0|νL′⟩. In the review’s convention, the rate contribution is

kVSC=2|Δ|2e−βω0∫0∞dωJrev(ω)A0(ω−ω0).
(36)

The normalized transition line shape A0 accounts for broadening of the reactive transition. The Boltzmann factor is the activated approximation used in the review; a general thermal upward rate retains the full Bose factor rather than replacing it by e−βω. Here the formula is quoted in the oscillator subsection’s ℏ=1 units.

At resonance, splitting the spectator response away from the reactive frequency reduces this overlap. In the narrow-line limit, the ratio is set by ImXBB(ω0) relative to its uncoupled value. At ωc=ω0, Π(ω0)=a2 and ΓR(ω0)=γ+a2/κc. When the coupling-induced damping dominates, the response at the original transition decreases approximately as a−2, subject to the stated line-width and coupling limits.

This is a reduction in access to an energy-promoting vibration. It is not an assertion that the potential barrier was raised by the optical splitting. The source’s comparisons and action spectra concern this modeled energy-flow route. Read the rate construction.

Section 34Background channels, alignment, and a finite bottleneck

The review separates a background contribution from the spectator-mediated route: k=kD+αkVSC. Let b=kD/k0 be the fraction of the uncoupled rate carried by the unaffected background, and let r be the cavity-to-no-cavity ratio of the bright spectral overlap. Including reaction–optical alignment χ, a simple channel mixture gives

kk0=b+(1−b)[(1−χ)+χr].
(37)

This expression assumes independent additive channels with unchanged weights. It is a transparent teaching generalization of the aligned model, not a universal phenomenological law. At χ=0, the optical modification is invisible to the reaction. At strong suppression r→0, the surviving background and dark reaction routes prevent the total rate from vanishing.

A different limitation comes from the sequential mechanism νL→νL′→νR′→νR. For irreversible independent waiting times with rates k1,k2,k3, the inverse mean completion time is

kcompletion=(1k1+1k2+1k3)−1.
(38)

Only when k1≪k2,k3 does this reduce to the initial vibrational excitation rate. If another step is slow, modifying k1 may have little influence. Reversible intermediate steps require a first-passage or kinetic-matrix calculation; simply multiplying several rate constants is dimensionally and physically wrong.

Section 35Why a kinetic effect need not imply a new equilibrium barrier

For any fixed spectator coordinates, the classical photonic partition integral in this model can be shifted:

∫−∞∞dqcexp⁡[−βωc22(qc+aωcRB)2]=2πβωc2,
(39)

which is independent of RB and the coupling. The unrestricted spectator coordinate integrals can likewise be shifted for fixed R0. Thus these classical coordinate-square terms alone do not alter the equilibrium potential of mean force along R0, even though they alter dynamical energy flow. This argument uses classical phase-space integration, unbounded harmonic coordinates, and the complete counterterms. It is not a blanket statement about quantum equilibrium, anharmonicity, or arbitrary cavity Hamiltonians.

Converting an observed rate ratio into ΔΔGapparent‡=−kBTln⁡(k/k0) defines an apparent kinetic penalty. It does not prove that a microscopic potential-energy barrier changed. Likewise, changing one forward kinetic channel without a consistent backward channel does not establish an equilibrium constant modification.

Section 36Normal incidence and the dimensionality of the photonic continuum

For a planar cavity, ω(k)=vk⊥2+k2, with v the in-medium light speed and ωc=vk⊥. A density of modes in d in-plane dimensions follows from ρd(ω)dω∝kd−1dk, giving

ρd(ω)∝ω(ω2−ωc2)(d−2)/2,ω≥ωc.
(40)

In one in-plane dimension the ideal density has a threshold divergence; in two it has a finite step proportional to ω. It is therefore not correct to invoke the same divergent normal-incidence density in every geometry. Finite size, excitation selection, escape paths, polarization, and mode-dependent lifetime determine what spectral weight is actually sampled.

The review discusses normal-incidence selectivity in the kinetic framework. The density-of-states calculation here is an additional geometry check: a single-mode response calculator cannot by itself establish the angular selectivity of a real multimode experiment.

Section 37Explore the spectator-response mechanism numerically

This calculator inverts the damped bright/photon response matrix. It integrates its positive-frequency imaginary part against a normalized Gaussian reactive line shape and compares the result with the uncoupled spectator. All frequency-like inputs use the same cm−1 scale; common conversion factors cancel in the ratio. The reported normal frequencies are those of the undamped coordinate-square Hamiltonian.

The two numerical grids are compared before the result is accepted. Narrow peaks may require greater resolution than a small browser calculator can afford; it then reports a convergence warning instead of pretending to have an exact integral. The temperature-dependent prefactor, the reaction matrix element, and the common spectral normalization cancel in this particular ratio. Consequently the output is not an absolute reaction rate.

Vibrational response and a kinetic-overlap ratio

Section 38How the two VSC discussions on this website differ

The ARPC mechanism just derived treats cavity-coupled spectator oscillators, their effect on a reactive vibrational spectral density, and a rate-limiting energy-flow step. The separate Nature Communications VSC Deep Dive develops a proposed macroscopic condensation construction using an effective many-body vibrational exchange model and a variational treatment.

Both address collective VSC, but they do not use the same elimination, statistical assumption, or rate mechanism. A success or limitation of one is not automatically evidence for or against the other. In particular, the susceptibility calculation above does not derive a condensation threshold, and the variational gap is not to be inserted without derivation as a linewidth in the spectator response.

For a reader entering from the review, this distinction is important: a review organizes multiple explanations and their scope; it should not be read as claiming that all observed kinetic changes already have one established microscopic origin.

Section 39A connected reading of the review’s figures

Figure What it illustrates What to test before extending the conclusion
Figure 1, PDF p. 3 Optical hybridization and the landscape of excitonic/vibrational strong coupling Whether the relevant material, observable, and excitation regime match the model
Figure 2, PDF p. 6 Bright/dark structure and projected nuclear displacement Diagonal averaging versus residual off-diagonal bath transitions
Figure 3, PDF p. 10 Coherence, absorption, and subaverage linewidths Line shape, bare width convention, bath time scale, and fitted versus derived formulas
Figure 4, PDF p. 12 Collective electron transfer and detuning competition Prepared-state rate versus pumped flux or product yield
Figure 5, PDF p. 15 Spectator-assisted VSC kinetic mechanism Rate-limiting step, background channel, alignment, and oscillator counterterms

The review itself credits the underlying studies. This tutorial links to those review discussions rather than claiming to rerun or independently validate every cited experimental dataset. The calculations supplied below reproduce the tutorial’s finite matrices and limiting identities, not the literature’s full figures.

Section 40Numerical checks and downloadable teaching code

Download collective_effects_teaching.py

python collective_effects_teaching.py --test
python collective_effects_teaching.py --rates --output collective_rates.csv
python collective_effects_teaching.py --spectator --output spectator_response.csv

The script requires NumPy. It constructs bright/dark transformations, checks local projector identities and channel sums, verifies detailed balance in a probability-conserving kinetic matrix, evaluates the Marcus expression, and independently compares the analytic spectator susceptibility with a direct complex matrix inverse. The spectator output includes both coupled and uncoupled responses and the reactive Gaussian weighting.

It does not perform electronic-structure calculations, ab initio dynamics, HEOM, full nonlinear spectroscopy, or production chemical-kinetics fitting. Its purpose is to make the review’s different levels of approximation independently testable. A test can verify an algebraic implementation while leaving the physical adequacy of its model an open question.

Section 41Validity and interpretation checklist

Before using a formula from the review, write down the space, observable, and approximation. The bright-state diagonalization is exact within a uniform rank-one excitation Hamiltonian. Projected reorganization uses independent harmonic baths and a chosen branch. FGR rates additionally use weak coupling and equilibrium bath statistics. A secular rate matrix discards coherences. Marcus theory adds a classical Gaussian solvent and a weak electronic transition. The oscillator response is exact only for its damped linear model; translating it into chemistry assumes a particular bottleneck and transition line shape.

Finite excitation density, saturation, correlated disorder, many cavity modes, collective intermolecular electrostatics, ultrastrong coupling, and genuine quantum equilibrium each introduce new issues. They cannot be resolved by retaining the same formula and renaming its coupling parameter.

The most useful outcome of the review is therefore a collection of mechanism-specific tests: derive the local matrix element, sum the correct final channels, check detailed balance and probability conservation, specify fixed g or fixed G, and distinguish a rate from a yield and a kinetic penalty from an equilibrium free energy.

Section 42Exercises with worked solutions

1. Construct the bright ket for unequal couplings

Take two molecules with real couplings g1=3 and g2=4 in the same energy unit. Then G=5, |B⟩=(3|E1⟩+4|E2⟩)/5, and one normalized dark ket is |D⟩=(4|E1⟩−3|E2⟩)/5. Directly applying the photon row gives ⟨c|H^|D⟩=(12−12)/5=0. For identical molecular energies, the bright/photon splitting at resonance is 10, not 22 times either individual coupling.

2. Compare fixed individual and fixed collective coupling

At fixed g, increasing N from 100 to 400 doubles G=Ng. At fixed G, it halves g. In the latter comparison the ideal polariton energies and fractions stay the same, but independent-bath reorganization decreases by four. In the former comparison the energy gaps also change, so FGR rates sample a different part of the bath spectrum. These are physically different scans.

3. Verify a projected local bath matrix

For the resonant dimer, the row of site-1 components in the (+,−,D) basis is (1/2,−1/2,1/2). Its outer product gives [n^1]+,−,D. Squaring that matrix returns itself because the row has unit norm. Its trace is one and its eigenvalues are (1,0,0), even though all three diagonal entries are nonzero. A projector need not be diagonal in every basis.

4. Find the common-noise floor

For w=1/2, N=1000, and r=0.01, the variance factor is w2[r+(1−r)/N]=0.25(0.01099)=0.0027475. Independent noise would give 0.00025. A seemingly small common correlation therefore dominates at large N. The large-N floor is 0.0025, not zero.

5. Recover the dark-manifold overlap without choosing every dark ket

Completeness gives ∑j|unDj|2=⟨En|P^D|En⟩=1−1/N. Multiply by the upper-polariton weight w+/N on site n and sum over n: the result is w+(N−1)/N. This projector proof works without explicitly constructing the N−1 Fourier dark states.

6. Repair a thermal rate by a zero-temperature test

As T→0, n¯(ΔE)→0. Upward thermal excitation should vanish, but a downward transition can emit a phonon into the vacuum. Therefore the downward factor must be n¯+1. Assigning n¯ to both upward and downward rates makes both vanish and violates detailed balance at finite temperature. This simple limit detects the printed Equation 13c issue.

7. Check the equilibrium dark/lower ratio

Set N=11 and Δ−=kBTln⁡10. Then PD/PL=10e−ln⁡10=1. Each dark state has population PL/10, so the total dark population equals the lower-polariton population. The quantity kBTln⁡10 is a degeneracy-related free-energy contribution, not the energy of ten independent excitations.

8. Distinguish cavity width and optical coherence time

For W=10 meV and ℏ=658.21196 meV fs, the photon population lifetime is 65.8212 fs. The isolated optical coherence time is 131.6424 fs. Its energy FWHM is still 10 meV, since 2ℏ/T2=10 meV. Confusing population and amplitude damping creates a factor-of-two linewidth error.

9. Find a Marcus activationless point

Let ΔG=0, λA=100 meV, and zero detuning. Then ΔE+=G, and the activationless condition is G=100 meV. At G=200 meV the exponent becomes −1002/(4×100×kBT), equal to its value at G=0 if the prefactor is held fixed. The rate maximum is not at unlimited coupling.

10. Compute a yield and identify the missing channel

For kA=2, kD=3, and kc=5 ps−1, the product yield is 2/10=0.2. The upper population lifetime is 0.1 ps. A model that reports only kA has not predicted the yield. If dark population later returns, the absorbing-dark assumption fails and a kinetic matrix must replace this simple branching fraction.

11. Check the dipole-self-energy determinant

For ω0=ωc=1 and a=2, the full matrix is (5221), whose determinant is one and whose eigenvalues are 3±8>0. Omitting the self-energy gives (1221) with eigenvalues 3 and −1. The imaginary normal frequency in the latter is a changed-model artifact, not the result of the coordinate-square Hamiltonian.

12. Calculate exact resonant oscillator frequencies

For equal bare frequencies ω0, the positive roots obey ω+−ω−=a and ω+ω−=ω02. Therefore ω±=(4ω02+a2±a)/2. For ω0=1000, a=80 in a common frequency scale, they are approximately 1040.7997 and 960.7997. The splitting is 80, while the mean is 1000.7997 rather than exactly 1000.

13. Test a susceptibility at zero coupling

Set a=0. Then Π=0, ΓR=γ, and XBB=1/(ω02−ω2−iγω), independent of the cavity frequency and loss. The integrated cavity/no-cavity spectral ratio must be one for every positive reactive line shape. Both the browser calculator and the Python tests check this limit.

14. Account for a dark reaction route

Take an unaffected fraction b=0.2, alignment χ=0.25, and strongly reduced bright overlap r=0.1. Then k/k0=0.2+0.8(0.75+0.025)=0.82. Although the bright route is suppressed by 90%, the overall reaction is reduced by only 18%. A large optical splitting alone gives no estimate of the overlap χ.

15. Compare a fast and slow first step

With (k1,k2,k3)=(1,100,100), the inverse mean completion time is 1/1.02≃0.9804, close to k1. With (100,1,100), it has the same value but is limited by k2. Halving k1 in the second system changes the denominator from 1.02 to 1.03, only about a one-percent effect. A cavity-sensitive step must also be kinetically important.

16. Show why a shifted photon coordinate leaves the classical integral unchanged

Use y=qc+aRB/ωc. The Jacobian is one and the integration limits stay (−∞,∞). The Gaussian integral depends only on βωc2, not RB or a. The result relies on the whole square. Expanding it and then discarding the a2RB2/2 term prevents this cancellation and changes the equilibrium model.

Section 43Further reading within this website

The review connects most naturally to the motional-narrowing derivation, efficient collective propagation, nonlinear response and importance sampling, PNAS coherence and 2DES, atomistic classical-path transport, and the distinct macroscopic VSC proposal.

The main source is Ying et al., ARPC 77, 201–224 (2026). Its reference list identifies the original theories and experiments behind each reviewed result. These notes use the full review PDF; the additional elementary examples and response calculations are derived here and are not presented as new results of the original review.
